author: Jeremy Jones
title: Photo exhibit spotlights Hispanic Valley history - NewsBreak
text:
By Jeremy Jones ,
1 hours ago
YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio (WKBN) – As we celebrate Hispanic Heritage Month, a new photo exhibit at the Tyler History Center is spotlighting Youngstown’s vibrant Hispanic community.
When you walk into the newest exhibit at the Tyler History Center, pictures of Hispanic residents fill the walls. Photographer Tony Nicholas, who is also a professor at Youngstown State University, got the idea while taking pictures at his daughter’s graduation, and he realized all of her friends were Hispanic.
“Through the project of the last couple of years, I’ve learned I had friends but didn’t realize the vast size of the crown of community and that they’ve been here a long time. And for whatever reason, they just weren’t paid attention to. And it almost surprised me that this type of project hadn’t happened previously,” Nicholas said.
Nicholas named the exhibit “This is Youngstown,” showing how deep Latino roots are in the city, with family tracing their history in the Valley back generations. Many of the families worked in the steel mills and opened up local businesses. He says when the exhibit debuted, many were filled with tears of joy to have representation in a city they’ve lived in for generations.
“That’ll put a tear in your eyes. I had people at the opening Friday with tears in their eyes. They were just thrilled that this was happening. That’s a good feeling that photography — that it describes, but it also tells us who we are. I try to give that to everyone I photograph. There’s little things you do to give them their power — they’re there,” Nicholas said.
The exhibit features nearly 40 portraits, and all of them have a story behind each person in the picture. Nicholas says his goal is to show not only the vibrant Hispanic community in Youngstown, but also to remind people that this community is a big one. They have roots, wake up and go to work, and raise families just like anyone else in the Valley.
“They’re all vital to this machine called Youngstown. It just keeps going. They are just like the rest of us. They get up and they go, do things, and sometimes they might not want to do it, but that’s who they are. They contribute,” Nicholas said.
The exhibit debuted on Friday, October 3, but it will stay in the Tyler History Center until February. However, the pictures will forever remain a part of the Center’s collection.
“They will be forever. These people that are here, when they are long gone, their great-grandkids can come here and look at them and say, ‘This is what they look like,'” Nicholas said.
